title: Ghosts of the Past
subtitle: Beneath the earth, those who were never granted marble nor memorials call out her name.

content.text: Ahem ... Take a deep breath, soldier; the smoke's cleared now. This story—this "battle"—will soon come to an end.
A writer has departed from her domain, leaving her creations scattered behind her, like blood-soaked bandages and fragmented skulls in the trenches.
I don't understand it at all.

branch.text: Glad we're on the same page. Thank heavens my commander wasn't some kind of littérateur; else I'd have been blown to bits before I could decipher their poetic orders.

*whistle* How wonderful for you. You know what? You should be the leader of the Literature Encryption Communication Team. Just arm yourself with a dictionary, and even enemies with .45 Maxim machine guns won't stand a chance against you.
Because the poetry you recite will surely blow their minds before their bullets pierce yours.
You've developed a sense of humor.

Well, it's all thanks to a certain writer, the embodiment of the wandering poet and traveler from Santiago to Buenos Aires. She impressed me with her precious experience as a cafe dishwasher and campground caretaker.
What really rekindled my sense of humor was her seriousness about her literary pursuits. You'd understand what I mean if you'd ever heard a cheesy joke at a comrade's graveside.
Drawing strength from her wanderings and rebellious exploits, she attempted to change society, wielding the sword of literature as a revolutionary intellectual and a leader of thought.
Some would hail her as a battle angel of Latin America, with words as piercing as bullets and poems as powerful as tactical bombers.
I doubt literature has such a profound impact.
Many share your doubt, myself included.
You stand firm in your beliefs, huh? Well, maybe that's a good thing. A commander has to trust their soldiers, or they'll be forced to surrender before long.
Here, come closer. Let me tell you a secret ...
Many—if not all—people foolishly think it's the executioner who drops the guillotine blade, the powder that fires the bullet.

While they're half right, they're substantially inaccurate. The craters on the battlefield aren't the result of bombs, but of clashing ideologies—a trigger pulled long before the powder ever ignited in the barrel.
Well, it's probably best not to buy too much into the Latin American Boom. Forget about the status report from earlier.
That said, at least there's one thing that's certain:
Books can bite back—and they'll leave scars.
I believe in the power of literature.

items.text: Ghosts of the Past
On an unknown night, the wind carries the cold desolation of the desert.
In the cottage with a blue roof, a girl dreams of a circular prison.
Then, she wakes.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: What a bizarre dream.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: The taste of reality—so bitter and sad.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: But full of dialectical thinking, haha. Maybe the people of the Panopticon were reflecting my inner thoughts?
She looks around, surveying the cobwebbed corners where stacks of manuscripts have piled up to the ceiling and over empty ink bottles collecting dust.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Ah, so I really am a character in the novel!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: The mysterious cottage with the blue roof was my home all along. Then, the rumors the ghosts spread were indeed just that—rumors.
The young writer steps out of her home and into the streets of the familiar yet foreign desert town.
Countless nameless characters and ghosts arrive upon hearing the news, filling the roads and skies.

items.speaker: The Bank Clerk
items.text: Welcome back to Amalfitano, dear writer!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Thank you, dear icon of capitalism. But, didn't I tear this novel to pieces?
A woman wearing a peculiar hat steps forward.

items.speaker: The Paracausality Researcher
items.text: You see, Amalfitano is a dimension beyond life and death.

items.speaker: The Paracausality Researcher
items.text: This town is a reflection of your inner thoughts. It's incorporeal. You can't tear something incorporeal into pieces.

items.speaker: The Paracausality Researcher
items.text: Literature is endless and timeless, like a river flowing across life and death.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: No wonder you're my favorite character. You never cease to enlighten me.

items.speaker: The Door-Side Beggar
items.text: Unfortunately, literature is a dangerous and futile calling. Nobody truly understands or even remembers your work!

items.speaker: The Door-Side Beggar
items.text: Do you remember the saying? "The only truly dead are those who have been forgotten."

items.speaker: The Door-Side Beggar
items.text: Hahaha, Recoleta, you'll disappear for good if you leave Amalfitano again. It'll be like you never existed!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I've always admired your critical thinking, sir. It fits your role perfectly.
Rough hands grasp the writer's palm, feeling at the lines etched into her skin.

items.speaker: The Blind Weaver
items.text: Everything will be alright, Recoleta.

items.speaker: The Blind Weaver
items.text: Whatever happened, you've returned now. That's what matters.

items.speaker: The Blind Weaver
items.text: The Die of Babylon will roll again, and each of us will get our endings.
The crowd erupts in cheers.

items.speaker: The Murdered Donkey Driver
items.text: That's right. Solve the murder at the bar and put my soul at rest!

items.speaker: The Dune Piscator
items.text: Free the village from the madness inflicted by the ancient spirit!

items.speaker: The Paracausality Researcher
items.text: Fix the randomness of the Die of Babylon and flatten the calamitous frequency!

items.speaker: Amalfitano Residents
items.text: Roll the Die one last time, Recoleta!
The young writer takes a step forward. Everyone, the living and the ghosts, watches expectantly.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: So the ending I've been searching for is the one the other "me" was unable to give me?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: The "me" that plunged headfirst into the struggle against an undefeatable power. The "me" who ultimately left this land ...

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: After all this time, I've finally found my ending.
She grasps the gleaming Die of Babylon.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Just one more roll, and it will all be over.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: My story, my town ... Everything will finally come to an end.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: But the dream about the Panopticon ... It'll end as well, won't it?
She stops.

items.speaker: The Bank Clerk
items.text: Oh, sweetheart, it's just a dream.

items.speaker: The Door-Side Beggar
items.text: Ha, don't tell me you're abandoning your lifelong pursuit for a measly dream!

items.speaker: The Murdered Donkey Driver
items.text: That dream is cruel. No one understands this great novel there or this amazing town.

items.speaker: The Blind Weaver
items.text: But here, you are a true writer. This is your home, Recoleta.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: But I already miss my friends in that dream. It exists, just like this place does.

items.speaker: The Dune Piscator
items.text: But we're your friends too, Recoleta!

items.speaker: The Paracausality Researcher
items.text: You might disappear forever if you leave Amalfitano. Are you sure you want to leave?
The young writer puts down the die in her hand.
The die that signifies the end of everything vanishes into the sandy wind.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: You know what I'm like, my dear friends. I've spent my life embarking on foolish, unrewarded adventures.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: That's just who I am, isn't it?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Amalfitano is indeed an ideal place—a place for wandering, for a short trip, and for losing oneself for a while.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: And it has you, my fictional friends, who I love so dearly.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: But I must return to my dream and see my friends there. They're just as important to me.
As they hear her words, the ghosts of the town smile with relief.

items.speaker: The Paracausality Researcher
items.text: Yes, you're right, Recoleta.

items.speaker: The Paracausality Researcher
items.text: There's no denying that you're a noble and passionate soul. Every one of us knows it.

items.speaker: The Door-Side Beggar
items.text: Hmph, you're our dear friend, too. Why would we stop you from doing what you truly want?
Everyone makes way for her as a path into a boundless void unfolds.

items.speaker: The Blind Weaver
items.text: We wish you the very best, Recoleta.

items.speaker: The Blind Weaver
items.text: Goodnight, my dear. May your dream be a sweet one this time.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Thank you all, my friends. I'll never forget you.
The girl wipes the tears from her eyes and steps into the looming darkness.
All is silent as she enters the barren land. There is only the faint sound of footsteps echoing against a vast and empty darkness.

items.speaker: Editor
items.text: I've read your work, Ms. Recoleta. To be frank, it lacks both depth and breadth.

items.speaker: Editor
items.text: This town of yours is still far from reflecting the complexity of society, and the narrative lacks a discerning perspective. It still needs some work if you want it to truly resonate with our audience.

items.speaker: Editor
items.text: Just go for it, Miss. You're at a perfect age to explore, experience, and learn!
Time wheels, and at last the girl feels her existence again within the void. She reclaims her voice.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Wh-What's happening to me?
A thousand, or perhaps countless, faces emerge before her again.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Ah, of course! The Rise and Fall of Sanity is my story.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: So, even though the novel's been destroyed, the story—and myself along with it—lives on in the minds of those who read it.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Thank you for your feedback, editor! Even here in this great expanse of darkness, I can still hear your words!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: You have my gratitude. Thank you for reading my novel, even if you didn't understand it and likely never will.
She navigates a labyrinth of words and an endless expanse of mirrored waters. The darkness surging toward her like a rush of waves on a dark night, making her presence feel heavier.

items.speaker: Young Woman
items.text: Honestly, I find your story totally fascinating! But I'm still struggling to understand the connections between all these nameless characters. Couldn't you make it clearer, like a movie?

items.speaker: Young Man
items.text: Hmph, typical—trust a writer to try to be all obscure and mysterious.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: María, Pancho, you guys are the best traveling pals I've ever had!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Our paths may diverge in the future, but the joyful memories of our journey across grasslands, snowfields, and deserts together will remain forever.

items.speaker: Young Woman
items.text: It's been great coming along with you. You're totally one of a kind. We'll be waiting for you at my aunt's vineyard. A little sun after a hard day's work will do you good.
The passionate companions wave to her, never looking back as they continue forward. The girl's steps are no longer weightless. With every step she takes, they feel heavier and more real.
She lingers inside the infinite Mask in the Mirror, the boundless universe filling her with both confusion and illusion.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: There is ambition in her writing. It's passionate and poetic, fractured and chaotic. But, when viewed as a whole, her work feels like little more than a superficial illusion. It lacks the depth to truly touch the soul.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: I will refrain from offering further comments until she stops romanticizing her childish adventures.

items.speaker: The Physician
items.text: To put it bluntly, her phraseology feels overly deliberate to the point of distortion. Her verbiage is like a collection of vague sentiment bubbles.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I see, Aleph. Then this is how you really feel about my novel?

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: A thousand readers will interpret a story a thousand different ways. Some believe the text itself is dead, and it is the reader who gives it life.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: The truth cannot be fully conveyed through words alone. That said, I think The Rise and Fall of Sanity is a good story.
Her heart skips a beat.
Within this "paradise" that harbors the boundless histories and mysteries of humanity, she finally finds the mirror that shows her reality as it truly is.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Oh, so the eternal paradise is a library of sorts, just like I always imagined! Or, is this just another reflection of my inner thoughts?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Hmm, I like it here. It's nice being surrounded by literature.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: But it's time to go back. Back to reality.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: You're right about literature, Door-Side Beggar. It is a dangerous and futile calling, but I still believe in it.
The investigators from the Foundation breathe a sigh of relief together.
Recoleta's reappearance is as sudden as her disappearance. Sonetto hasn't even had time to wipe the tears from the corners of her eyes.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Recoleta? You're back!

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: I'm so glad to see you're safe.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: And I'm so glad to see you two worried sick about me, tee-hee! Thanks, my best friends Sonetto and Vertin!
The reborn writer turns to the prisoner sitting dejected nearby.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: See, Aleph? I still exist.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: Amalfitano is gone. It's all over.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: You're simply a wandering ghost now, never to return home again.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: You may still exist, but Amalfitano will never get its ending. You've nullified its existence, rendering all of this meaningless.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: I'm sorry I couldn't answer your question. I've failed once again.
His die falls to the ground. Once used to construct a beautiful dream, now whatever magic it held has dissipated.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: Amalfitano and the Panopticon were two parts of a whole.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: With Amalfitano gone, Comala no longer has any reason to exist.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I'm sorry, Aleph. You, who know all the mysteries of the world, who seek answers to every question,

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: have lost yourself in the process.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: You can answer everyone else's questions, but never your own.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Who's the person behind that mask? Is he real? Does he still exist?

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: Who am I?
The weighty ending to the story leaves the prisoner, still trapped in a blurred illusion, exhausted.
Comala Prison groans, like an aging waterwheel struggling under its own weight, distorting, fading, and collapsing into the currents of his mind.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Stay vigilant, everyone. This is just like when the Idealist and the Physician had their meltdown.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Only this time, it seems even worse.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I think ... Aleph is trying to tear down the Panopticon.
Beyond the crumbling walls, a shivering figure is faintly visible. He grips a gun tightly. The black barrel, shaking in his hands, is aimed at the people in the room.
F-Freeze! Stay where you are, all of you!
